title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context: §§1–2 (previous page) gave the equilibrium of an inextensible elastic rod EY in a plane. External elementary forces P ds, Q ds act in the x and y directions on each element. The bending moment at Y equals V times the change of curvature, with V the 'absolute elasticity' (flexural rigidity EI). Taking moments about Y gives ∫dy∫P ds − ∫dx∫Q ds = V(dy ddx − dx ddy)/ds³ − V/ρ, where 1/ρ is the natural curvature. The tangential tension is −(dx/ds)∫P ds − (dy/ds)∫Q ds.

On this page (Lemma 2, Solution) Euler passes to motion. The coordinates x(s,t), y(s,t) are treated as functions of two variables: the material arc length s from the end E, and the time t in seconds. Euler introduces parentheses (ddx/dt²), (ddy/dt²) to mark partial second derivatives in t with s held fixed; this is his standard partial-derivative notation. He then applies d'Alembert's principle by replacing the applied force densities with effective ones:
- P' = P − (S/2g) x_tt
- Q' = Q − (S/2g) y_tt
Here S ds is the weight of the element and g is the distance fallen in the first second, so 2g is the gravitational acceleration and S/2g is the mass per unit length.

The instantaneous configuration then satisfies the same moment equation with P', Q' in place of P, Q:
∫dy∫P' ds − ∫dx∫Q' ds = V(dy ddx − dx ddy)/ds³ − V/ρ.
The last term drops for a naturally straight rod (ρ = ∞). The tension is likewise −x_s∫P' ds − y_s∫Q' ds. Together these constitute the full nonlinear (large-deflection) equations of planar motion of an inextensible Euler–Bernoulli rod, without rotatory inertia, in integrated (moment) form; integrals run from the free end E.

Problem I (§4) begins the specialization: a uniform, naturally straight rod of given length EF, which on the next page is linearized to the small-vibration beam equation.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The formulation tacitly neglects rotatory inertia of the cross-sections (standard for Euler).
The formulation tacitly assumes inextensibility (s is a material arc length).
The moment equation holds as written only if the integrals ∫P' ds, ∫Q' ds are taken from the free end E, with any finite end forces included, as stated in §2.
Within the moment equation the differentials d are with respect to s at fixed t. This is implicit and not stated.

ideas.what: Applying d'Alembert's principle (subtracting mass × acceleration from applied forces) to convert the static elastica equations into dynamic ones
ideas.modern_name: d'Alembert's principle / inertial body forces in rod dynamics
ideas.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert (1743); for continua, Euler and Daniel Bernoulli
ideas.where_published: Euler E481 'Genuina principia...' (1774) and earlier vibrating-string and rod papers

ideas.what: Nonlinear dynamic equations of a planar inextensible elastic rod with natural curvature 1/ρ, moment proportional to change of curvature
ideas.modern_name: Kirchhoff/Euler dynamic elastica (planar Kirchhoff rod without rotatory inertia), intrinsically curved rod
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 elastica; 1770s general equations); Kirchhoff (1859) for the general 3D theory
ideas.where_published: E481 (1774); discussed in Truesdell, 'The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788' (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Notation (ddx/dt²) in parentheses for partial derivatives with the other variable held constant
ideas.where_published: Many Euler papers, e.g. Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 3

ideas.what: Tension in the rod expressed from the integrated effective forces projected on the tangent
ideas.modern_name: axial force resultant in rod theory

deep.surprise_reason: Standard Eulerian derivation of the dynamic rod equations via d'Alembert's principle. It is already discussed by Truesdell, and E526 itself is a known source for the beam vibration equation; nothing on this page is absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. The image shows 'dt²' in the denominator of the first fraction of P' (partly blurred as 'dt·') — consistent with the transcription.
